selection_rule: top-k species by (n_distinct_proposers, n_members, stable sha256); representative = member with smallest sha256(pid)

selected.name: Alternative comparison
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the comment compares the requested approach with feasible alternatives using explicit criteria such as effectiveness, burden, risk, or consistency; score 0 when no alternative is considered.
selected.rationale: R12 compares size limits with bag limits, and R11 compares multiple ways to report unknown amounts.
member_names: Contests the proposal's premise, necessity or legal basis

New information added beyond registering a bare position
Pinpoint citation to the specific provision under comment
Shows evidence of having read this particular document
Specific actionable recommendation or proposed rule text
Stays on the docket rather than drifting into grievance
Topical focus and freedom from digression

selected.name: Uncertainty calibration
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the comment distinguishes established facts, inferences, unknowns, and needed evidence and proposes how uncertainty could be resolved; score 0 when speculation is presented as certainty.
selected.rationale: R02 questions whether the proposed sample can answer the research question, and R50 asks for missing failure-rate comparisons rather than assuming them.

selected.name: Distributional Impact Analysis
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the comment examines how effects differ across multiple affected groups, especially vulnerable, geographically distinct, or less represented groups; score 0 when impacts are described only for the commenter.
selected.rationale: R17 discusses drivers across ages and experience levels, R26 addresses fishermen’s subsistence and cultural needs, and R54 quantifies consequences for passenger-vehicle occupants.

selected.name: Argument-carried weight vs. appeal to institutional size
selected.instruction: Score whether the comment's persuasive force rests on the substance of its reasoning and evidence, as opposed to resting on an implicit appeal to the submitting organization's size, membership count, or market share (e.g., citing '1,500 member companies' or '225,000 employees' as if that were itself the argument). A 10 relies entirely on reasoned, evidence-based argument. A 0 substitutes recitation of organizational scale or authority for actual argument.
selected.rationale: R14, R17, R20, and R51 (NAMIC and State Farm letters) each open with statistics about membership size, market share, or policy counts (e.g., 'more than 1,500... member companies,' 'over 40 million active automobile insurance policies') as the primary credential-establishing move before offering comparatively thin substantive analysis. All four are dense_high_card_low, suggesting the dense model may be responsive to this authority signal in a way a criteria-based scorer is not.
member_names: Argument carried by specifics, not by asserted credentials
Argument-carried weight vs. appeal to institutional size

selected.name: Mechanism-to-effect reasoning
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the comment explains a plausible chain from the proposed provision through an operational mechanism to a specific consequence; score 0 when it merely asserts that the proposal is good or harmful.
selected.rationale: R09 connects federal and nearshore closures to fishing impacts, and R32 explains how unsecured ambulance equipment becomes dangerous projectiles.

selected.name: Quantification of real-world stakes or impact
selected.instruction: Score the degree to which the comment supplies specific, checkable figures (dollar amounts, populations affected, physical quantities, percentages, casualty/injury counts, historical baselines) that let the reader gauge the magnitude of the rule's consequences. A 10 gives multiple specific, well-attributed figures tied directly to the argument. A 0 offers only vague qualitative claims ('a lot,' 'many,' 'significant harm') with no quantification at all.
selected.rationale: R45 (Truck Safety Coalition) anchors its argument in specific figures -- 5,700 deaths, 155,000 injuries, $66 billion in losses, a 71% increase since 2009 -- and R47 (American Samoa DMWR) sets the proposed 13,000-lb catch limit against a documented 21,139-lb five-year historical average. Both are dense_high_card_low, suggesting the dense model rewards this kind of checkable quantification in a way the scorecard's bank currently does not fully capture.
member_names: Attaches magnitude to the burden or harm claimed
Quantification of real-world stakes or impact

selected.name: Original firsthand text vs. formulaic template language
selected.instruction: Score whether the comment's language is specific to this commenter's own situation and this particular docket, versus reading like a generic template that could be dropped into many different comment periods with minor edits. A 10 is clearly composed for this specific submission with situation-specific detail. A 0 reads as boilerplate (e.g., a generic extension-request form) with the docket number as the only customized element.
selected.rationale: R15, R24, R40, and R49 are all comment-period extension requests that follow a near-identical template (trade association credentials, complexity claim, requested number of days) -- all four are dense_low_card_high, suggesting the scorecard rewards this formulaic genre more than the dense model does, which may be picking up on its generic, reusable phrasing.
member_names: Original firsthand text vs. formulaic template language

selected.name: Applicability Boundaries
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the comment precisely identifies which products, units, populations, or circumstances are affected and which are not, with a reason for the distinction; score 0 when it treats materially different cases as interchangeable.
selected.rationale: R29 identifies the precise affected components absent from FedEx’s fleet, while R57 distinguishes overlapping actuator requirements and compliance periods.

selected.name: Short decisive comment from a directly exposed party
selected.instruction: Judge whether the comment's length is proportionate to what it has to say, given who is saying it. 10 = a short comment that states a definite position on a matter the commenter is unambiguously exposed to, and then stops - no padding, no restatement of the notice. 5 = length roughly matched to content. 0 = a long comment whose length comes from self-description, restatement of the agency's own notice, or hedged generalities, so that very few distinct claims are made per page. Length by itself is neither good nor bad; the ratio is what is scored.
selected.rationale: R33 is one sentence from Boeing concurring in an airworthiness directive on its own airplane and R36 is a short United Airlines concurrence naming its affected fleet; both are dense-high (.947, .898) at card .333 and .220, suggesting the scorecard reads brevity as thinness. R03 and R15 are two-sentence comments that each carry exactly one definite claim, at card .022 and .046. R02 and R56 are long, orderly and card-high while making few distinct claims.
member_names: Short decisive comment from a directly exposed party

selected.name: Technical substantiation vs. ideological/emotional characterization
selected.instruction: Score whether the comment's persuasive force rests on specific technical, factual, or legal substantiation, as opposed to resting primarily on ideological or emotionally loaded characterization (e.g., labeling a prior rule an 'attack,' 'illegal,' or a 'War on Coal') without corresponding technical detail to back the characterization. A 10 backs every strong characterization with specific technical or factual support. A 0 relies on charged rhetoric with little or no technical substantiation behind it.
selected.rationale: R11 (Murray Energy) characterizes the prior rule as a 'woefully misguided and irrational attack,' an 'illegal de facto ban,' and part of a 'War on Coal' -- strong rhetoric with comparatively little specific technical rebuttal in the visible text -- and is dense_high_card_low (dense_pct .826). By contrast R37 and R42 disagree just as forcefully with agency positions but do so through specific statutory citations and point-by-point technical rebuttal, suggesting rhetorical intensity untethered from substantiation may be something the dense model rewards that a criteria bank would not.

selected.name: Builds a record: exhibits, indexes, citations, companion filings
selected.instruction: Score the evidentiary apparatus the comment brings with it. 10 = footnoted sources, an index of attachments, named studies with authors, prior submissions in this or a related docket, or explicit cross-references to companion comments. 5 = one or two named sources. 0 = no sources, attachments or cross-references of any kind.
selected.rationale: R13 is nothing but a master index of dozens of attached studies and agency documents assembled for a CAFE docket, and R27 footnotes NHTSA, FMCSA, BLS and IIHS across a fifty-year history of agency inaction; R45 forwards companion NCGA and Missouri Corn comments. Card ranks these .205, .342 and .357 while the dense model ranks them .942, .964 and .945 - consistent with a scorecard scoring the visible page rather than the package that page introduces.
member_names: Builds a record: exhibits, indexes, citations, companion filings

selected.name: Disclosed firsthand expertise grounding the claims
selected.instruction: Score whether the commenter explicitly establishes personal, verifiable firsthand expertise or direct experience (credentials, years of hands-on practice, direct observation) that specifically grounds the technical claims made, as opposed to speaking from unstated or purely institutional authority. A 10 clearly discloses relevant credentials or experience that directly support the specific claims made. A 0 offers no such grounding -- claims stand on their own or on unstated authority.
selected.rationale: R03 opens by listing the commenter's A&P/IA mechanic certification, engineering degrees, and 6,000+ flight hours before making detailed technical claims about ELT failure rates; R19 grounds a fisheries argument in 30 years of firsthand charter fishing and a marine biology degree. Both are dense_low_card_high (R03 dense_pct .095, R19 dense_pct .164) despite the depth of disclosed expertise, suggesting the scorecard credits this kind of grounding more than the dense model does.
member_names: Disclosed firsthand expertise grounding the claims

selected.name: Content exceeds its packaging rather than the reverse
selected.instruction: Score the balance between presentational apparatus and delivered content. 10 = plain presentation carrying dense, non-redundant content. 5 = form and content matched. 0 = elaborate apparatus - numbered comment-response tables, formal headings, duplicated cover-and-attachment text, checkbox forms - wrapped around thin, purely editorial, or repeated content. Judge the apparatus against what it actually delivers, not against a general standard of tidiness.
selected.rationale: R51 presents ten comments in a formal comment-response table whose displayed entry is a checked 'Editorial' wording change, and R21 reproduces its entire three-sentence request verbatim twice, once as portal text and once as the attached letter; card ranks them .986 and .993, the two highest in the slice, while the dense model ranks them .173 and .129. R35 shows the same shape at card .934 with dense .075. R59 has no apparatus whatsoever and is dense .803 at card .189.
member_names: Content exceeds its packaging rather than the reverse

selected.name: Historical or precedential grounding of the request
selected.instruction: Score whether the comment situates its position within relevant regulatory history, prior agency actions, or precedent (e.g., citing how the agency handled comparable past dockets, or tracing the issue's history over time), as opposed to treating the current proposal in isolation with no historical context. A 10 explicitly and specifically grounds the argument in comparable precedent or history. A 0 offers no historical or precedential context at all.
selected.rationale: R40 (Al Fakher Tobacco) cites two specific prior ANPRM comment-period extensions (menthol, Docket FDA-2013-N-0521; NNN, Docket FDA-2016-N-2527) with exact day counts as precedent for its own request; R45 (Truck Safety Coalition) traces the agency's awareness of side-underride risk back to a specific 1969 statement, spanning over 50 years of inaction. Both ground otherwise simple requests in specific historical precedent, a property the current criteria set may not isolate.
member_names: Historical or precedential grounding of the request

selected.name: Technical precision achieved concisely (technical economy)
selected.instruction: Score the comment for combining (a) concrete, verifiable technical detail -- part numbers, dates, thresholds, section numbers -- with (b) brevity: no unnecessary padding, throat-clearing, or repetition. A 10 conveys precise technical content in the fewest words needed. A 0 either lacks technical precision, or buries whatever precision exists under substantial unrelated or repetitive padding.
selected.rationale: R39 (International Aero Engines) makes a precise, three-sentence technical request naming exact engine model numbers and a specific service bulletin; R33 (Japan Airlines) does the same in two sentences. Both are short and dense_low_card_high. By contrast R32 and R50 are long, repetitive, and technically imprecise despite being dense_high_card_low -- the interaction of precision AND concision appears to run opposite to how the two scores rank these rows.

selected.name: Organizational scale self-description
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how explicitly the text states the submitting organization's scale or resources -- e.g., a specific membership count, revenue figure, market-share percentage, or employee/customer count. 0 = no such scale statement anywhere in the text; 10 = the text prominently and repeatedly quantifies the organization's size. Do not judge whether the organization's size makes its argument more or less correct -- score only whether such a scale statement is present in the text.
selected.rationale: R22 and R51 (NAMIC) both state '1,500 member companies... $323 billion in annual premiums / 55 percent of the auto market'; R39 (UnitedHealth Group) states 'workforce of 225,000 people... 125 million people worldwide.' These scale claims are about the filer's resources, not the argument's merits, though a well-resourced filer may also genuinely produce more careful comments, which is why this is tagged mixed.

selected.name: OCR and transcription artifacts
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much scanning, OCR, transcription, encoding, character-substitution, spacing, or visible document-conversion error is present? Score only extent; do not judge whether the artifacts are good, bad, or indicative of substantive quality.
selected.rationale: Legacy scanning, email extraction, and conversion systems can leave mechanical traces that affect model behavior but have no substantive content value. Such artifacts are visible in R15 and R41, and also in R17 and R57.

selected.name: Technical identifier density
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the text uses specialized acronyms, model numbers, part numbers, docket identifiers, standards codes, or regulatory alphanumeric strings; do not judge whether the technical detail is correct.
selected.rationale: Identifier-heavy language may reflect topic, industry convention, or author specialization and can influence text processing independently of substantive quality. Examples include R20, R40, R45, and R59.
member_names: Density of technical identifiers and legal citation strings

selected.name: Legal/regulatory citation apparatus density
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text displays formal legal/regulatory citation apparatus -- numbered footnotes, pincites to the Federal Register/CFR/U.S.C., precise docket/RIN number recitation, or law-firm-style formal phrasing ('the undersigned', 'respectfully submits'). 0 = no such apparatus; 10 = dense, brief-style citation apparatus throughout. Do not judge whether the legal argument itself is correct -- score only the extent of this citation/formality apparatus.
selected.rationale: R31 (Ice Miller LLP) cites specific Treasury regulation subsections with case-style precision (e.g., '1.457-12(e)(2)(i)'); R35, R42, and R46 (extension-request letters from AFFI, ACC, and Consumer Brands) all carry footnoted Federal Register pincites. This apparatus signals professional/legal drafting support, which could reflect both a nuisance halo effect and genuinely more careful argumentation, hence mixed.

selected.name: Professional legal drafting
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the text uses lawyerly drafting conventions, formal legal framing, structured sections, defined terms, or counsel attribution; do not judge whether the drafting is good.
selected.rationale: Access to counsel or professional editors leaves recognizable drafting fingerprints that may affect reception independently of the underlying substance, while also potentially improving substance. Examples include R11, R33, R35, and R56.

selected.name: Professional production markers
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much formal letterhead, legal correspondence structure, contact information, document conventions, or polished signatory presentation is present? Score only extent; do not judge whether the production quality is good or whether the arguments are sound.
selected.rationale: Access to lawyers, regulatory staff, or professional editors can leave formal production traces that are not themselves substantive quality. These traces are prominent in R04 and R30, and also visible in R16.

selected.name: Scanned-attachment ingestion signature: stub, OCR garble, page furniture
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much of the item bears the marks of having been filed as a scanned or PDF attachment and then machine-transcribed, rather than typed directly into the comment box. Count, as extent: (a) a short transmittal stub at the top such as 'See attached', 'See attached file(s)', 'Please find attached', optionally preceded by a bare digit; (b) character-level transcription corruption -- dropped or doubled letters, letters substituted for each other, mangled signatures, ligature errors; (c) page furniture carried through from the source document -- 'Page 2 of 8', repeated date/addressee headers, fax and phone footers, stray line breaks mid-sentence; (d) duplication, where the same paragraph appears once in the cover note and again in the attachment body. Anchors: 0 = clean typed prose with none of these; 5 = clear stub plus page headers but readable text; 10 = pervasive corruption and page furniture that makes stretches hard to read. Do NOT judge whether the corruption makes the comment worse, and do NOT penalise or reward the author for it -- you are scoring how much of this signature is visible, nothing else.
selected.rationale: MODE 2. The unseen factor is how the document physically reached the docket -- faxed or mailed paper and scanned PDFs get OCR'd, inline web-form text does not -- and it leaves a loud textual fingerprint. R02 shows it as a mangled signature ('/)~ __ fivJ-', 'Gro~') and 'It_appears'; R09 (UPS Airlines) is corrupted throughout ('lowe e023 ups', 'flet', 'samme', 'ofthe'); R10 shows systematic character substitution ('ltr/ater Quality Standards', 'Ambient' rendered 'Ambientt'-style, 'W'atershed'); R33 renders every W as VV ('VVildEarth', 'FVVS'); R29's board roster is nearly unreadable. This is an artifact of the pipeline and of filing habits, not of the author's reasoning, yet it is a strong, stable, learnable text signal, and it co-varies with era and with paper-filing organisations. Tagged not-mixed because the corruption itself is injected downstream of the author and cannot make the underlying argument better.
member_names: Scanned-attachment ingestion signature: stub, OCR garble, page furniture
selected.upstream_parent: submission medium (paper/fax/scanned PDF attachment versus native electronic text entry), plus the corpus's own OCR pipeline
upstream_parent_all_members: submission medium (paper/fax/scanned PDF attachment versus native electronic text entry), plus the corpus's own OCR pipeline

selected.name: Comment-period timing/procedural request share
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much of this comment is a procedural request about timing (e.g., asking to extend the comment period) or an explicit statement about time pressure (e.g., referencing a holiday season or insufficient time to prepare), as opposed to comment on the substance of the proposed rule. 0 = entirely substantive comment on the rule, no timing/procedural content; 10 = the comment is entirely a timing/procedural request. Do not judge whether the timing request is reasonable or justified -- score only how much of the text is devoted to it.
selected.rationale: R35 (AFFI), R42 (ACC), R45 (PMI), and R46 (Consumer Brands) are each entirely a request to extend the comment period -- R42 explicitly invokes 'just after the Holiday Season' as its justification. None of the four engages the substance of the proposed rule at all; a criterion-based scorecard could easily reward the mere presence of a well-formed, on-topic procedural ask, while a reader looking for substantive engagement would not.

selected.name: Document volume
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much extended text, page-level elaboration, or multi-section material is present? Score only extent from the item text; do not judge whether the amount is good, persuasive, accurate, or relevant.
selected.rationale: Submission capacity and staff time can produce longer documents, independently of substantive merit. Extended multi-page material appears in R06 and R43, while much shorter comments appear in R12 and R44.

selected.name: Attachment-index / cover-page share of text
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much of the visible text functions as an index, cover page, or file-list pointing to separately attached material (e.g., filenames, 'Batch X of Y', 'See attached file(s)' immediately followed by a list of exhibit titles) rather than being the substantive comment itself. 0 = the visible text is entirely the substantive comment; 10 = the visible text is entirely an index/cover page for unseen attachments. Do not judge the value of the attachments themselves -- score only how much of the visible text is index/cover material.
selected.rationale: R04 (NRDC et al.) is literally a '[Batch 9 of 18]' master index of attachment filenames with no argument of its own; R16 and R23 both open with 'See attached file(s)' before the real letter begins, meaning part of the visible text is a pure attachment-pointer rather than comment.
